```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(eco)
  library(marked)
  library(R2ucare)
  library(data.table)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(plotly)
})
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
options(digits = 3)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")
```

An animal that is marked and never seen again either died or was alive and
missed. Those are two different coin flips, and the history of a single
animal cannot tell them apart. The Cormack-Jolly-Seber model (Cormack 1964;
Jolly 1965; Seber 1965) separates them by following many marked animals
over many occasions: an animal seen at occasion 5 was alive at occasions 2 to
4 whether or not it was seen there, and those known-alive misses estimate the
recapture probability $p$. Once $p$ is known, the disappearances that $p$
cannot explain are deaths, or emigrations, and estimate the survival
probability $\phi$. This page fits the model to one eco table, the European
dipper of Lebreton et al. (1992), and then to every capture-history table in
the warehouse, with `marked` doing the fitting.

::: {.callout-note}
This vignette, including the choice of tables, the analysis and the writing,
was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic) from a task specification, with
human review. Treat the interpretations accordingly; the code is all on the
page and runs from a clean session.
:::

## Try it first

Animals are marked at the first occasion. Between occasions each live animal
survives with probability $\phi$; at each occasion each live animal is seen
with probability $p$. Drag the sliders and watch the amber cells: those are
animals alive and missed, which a count of sightings reads as dead.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var ids = ["phi", "p", "k", "n"], el = {}, val = {};
  ids.forEach(function (k) { el[k] = document.getElementById("cjs-" + k); val[k] = document.getElementById("cjs-" + k + "-val"); });
  var grid = document.getElementById("cjs-grid");
  var out = {};
  ["true", "naive", "return", "phat", "missed"].forEach(function (k) { out[k] = document.getElementById("cjs-" + k); });
  var z = [], y = [];

  function simulate() {
    var phi = +el.phi.value, p = +el.p.value, K = +el.k.value, n = +el.n.value;
    z = []; y = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      z[i] = [1]; y[i] = [1];
      for (var t = 1; t < K; t++) {
        z[i][t] = (z[i][t - 1] === 1 && Math.random() < phi) ? 1 : 0;
        y[i][t] = (z[i][t] === 1 && Math.random() < p) ? 1 : 0;
      }
    }
  }

  function draw() {
    var phi = +el.phi.value, p = +el.p.value, K = +el.k.value, n = +el.n.value;
    val.phi.textContent = "φ = " + phi.toFixed(2);
    val.p.textContent = "p = " + p.toFixed(2);
    val.k.textContent = "K = " + K;
    val.n.textContent = "n = " + n;
    var html = "", atRisk = 0, survived = 0, kaNum = 0, kaDen = 0, returned = 0, seenKA = 0, missKA = 0, missedEnd = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      var last = 0;
      for (var t = 0; t < K; t++) if (y[i][t]) last = t;
      if (last > 0) returned++;
      for (var t = 0; t < K - 1; t++) {
        if (z[i][t]) { atRisk++; survived += z[i][t + 1]; }
        if (t <= last) { kaDen++; if (t + 1 <= last) kaNum++; }
      }
      for (var t = 1; t < last; t++) { if (y[i][t]) seenKA++; else missKA++; }
      if (z[i][K - 1] === 1 && last < K - 1) missedEnd++;
      var when = [];
      y[i].forEach(function (v, t) { if (v) when.push(t + 1); });
      var alive = z[i].reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0);
      var title = "animal " + (i + 1) + ": seen at " + when.join(", ") +
        "; " + (alive === K ? "alive at the end" : "died after occasion " + alive);
      html += '<div title="' + title + '" style="display:flex;gap:2px;padding:2px;border-radius:3px;">';
      for (var t = 0; t < K; t++) {
        var s;
        if (y[i][t]) s = "background:#1e8a5a;";
        else if (z[i][t] && t < last) s = "background:#ededea;border:1px solid #c9ccc8;box-sizing:border-box;";
        else if (z[i][t]) s = "background:repeating-linear-gradient(45deg,#c08a1e 0 2px,#fff 2px 4px);border:1px solid #c08a1e;box-sizing:border-box;";
        else s = "background:transparent;border:1px dashed #c9ccc8;box-sizing:border-box;";
        html += '<span style="display:inline-block;width:11px;height:14px;border-radius:2px;' + s + '"></span>';
      }
      html += "</div>";
    }
    grid.innerHTML = html;
    out["true"].textContent = (atRisk ? survived / atRisk : 0).toFixed(2) + "  (φ = " + phi.toFixed(2) + ")";
    out.naive.textContent = (kaDen ? kaNum / kaDen : 0).toFixed(2);
    out["return"].textContent = (returned / n).toFixed(2) + "  (" + returned + "/" + n + ")";
    out.phat.textContent = (seenKA + missKA ? (seenKA / (seenKA + missKA)).toFixed(2) : "–") + "  (" + missKA + " misses of " + (seenKA + missKA) + ")";
    out.missed.textContent = String(missedEnd);
  }

  ids.forEach(function (k) { el[k].addEventListener("input", function () { simulate(); draw(); }); });
  document.getElementById("cjs-resim").addEventListener("click", function () { simulate(); draw(); });
  simulate(); draw();
})();
</script>
```

Three things to notice. Naive survival, which reads every animal's last
sighting as its death, is always below $\phi$, and the gap closes only as
$p$ approaches 1. The grey cells give an estimate of $p$ that needs no model
at all, because an animal seen later was certainly alive: that is the whole
identification argument of CJS in one line. And the amber cells pile up at
the end of the study, where an animal has no later occasion to prove it was
alive; this is why the last survival and recapture probabilities in a fully
time-varying model cannot be separated.

## The model

Condition on animal $i$'s first capture, at occasion $f_i$. From then on it
carries a latent state $z_{it} \in \{0, 1\}$, alive or dead, that can only go
from 1 to 0,

$$
z_{i,t+1} \mid z_{it} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_{it}\, \phi_{it}^{\Delta_t}),
$$

where $\Delta_t$ is the time between occasions $t$ and $t+1$, so that $\phi$
is survival per unit of time (per year, below) whatever the spacing of the
surveys. Each occasion returns a sighting that is possible only when the
animal is alive,

$$
y_{it} \mid z_{it} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_{it}\, p_{it}).
$$

Summing the $z$s out gives the likelihood of one history. Up to the last
sighting $l_i$ the animal is known to be alive, so that part is a product of
survivals and of $p$ or $1-p$; after it, the animal either died or survived
and was missed, which is the probability $\chi_{l_i}$ of never being seen
again, defined backwards from the last occasion $K$:

$$
L_i = \prod_{t=f_i}^{l_i - 1} \phi_t^{\Delta_t} \, p_{t+1}^{y_{i,t+1}} (1 - p_{t+1})^{1 - y_{i,t+1}} \times \chi_{l_i},
\qquad
\chi_K = 1, \quad \chi_t = (1 - \phi_t^{\Delta_t}) + \phi_t^{\Delta_t} (1 - p_{t+1})\, \chi_{t+1}.
$$

The known-alive stretch informs $p$ directly. The tail $\chi$ is where
survival and detection are mixed together, and it is identified only
because $p$ has been pinned by the known-alive stretches of other animals.
With $\phi$ and $p$ both free at every occasion, the last pair appears only
as the product $\phi_{K-1} p_K$: the CJS version of the occupancy model's
"$J = 1$" problem.

::: {.callout-tip title="A psychometric reading"}
This is a hidden Markov model with an absorbing state, which makes it a
close cousin of a latent transition model with one irreversible transition:
the occasions are repeated items, $p$ is the item's endorsement probability
for respondents in the "alive" class, the dead class endorses nothing, and
$\phi$ is the probability of not dropping out. Read that way, the CJS model is
the dropout model of a longitudinal study in which dropout is unobserved:
a non-response may be a skipped wave or a respondent who is gone for good,
and the waves the respondent came back after tell you how often people skip.
Conditioning on first capture is conditioning on enrolment.
:::

## The data

The table is `lebreton_1992_dipper_cjs`: 294 European dippers (*Cinclus
cinclus*) marked in eastern France and recaptured each spring from 1981 to
1987, the dataset Lebreton, Burnham, Clobert and Anderson (1992) used to set
out the model-selection approach to capture-recapture, and the one that ships
with `marked`, RMark and MARK. Reads are pinned to eco version 10 so the
numbers on this page do not move when the warehouse grows.

```{r}
#| label: fetch
#| message: true
eco_set_version(10)
eco_info("lebreton_1992_dipper_cjs")
d <- as.data.table(eco_fetch("lebreton_1992_dipper_cjs"))
eco_periods("lebreton_1992_dipper_cjs")
head(d[order(unit, period)], 8)
```

One row per bird per year. `unit` is the bird, `period` the year's
capture session, `y` whether it was caught. The table carries a row for every
bird in every year from 1981, including years before it was first caught,
where `y` is 0: the standard keeps a row wherever the animal was at risk of
being recorded, and an unmarked bird is part of the population being
searched. CJS conditions on first capture, so those rows drop out of the
likelihood on their own.

```{r}
#| label: ch
M <- dcast(d, unit + unit_sex ~ period, value.var = "y")
ch <- data.frame(ch = apply(as.matrix(M[, -(1:2)]), 1, paste, collapse = ""),
                 sex = factor(M$unit_sex), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
table(captures = nchar(gsub("0", "", ch$ch)))
head(ch[nchar(gsub("0", "", ch$ch)) >= 3, ])
data(dipper, package = "marked")
identical(sort(ch$ch), sort(as.character(dipper$ch)))
```

The histories are the ones that ship with `marked`.

## Fitting

```{r}
#| label: fit-null
pr <- process.data(ch, model = "CJS", groups = "sex")
ddl <- make.design.data(pr)
fit <- function(phi, p) {
  invisible(capture.output(m <- crm(pr, ddl, hessian = TRUE,
    model.parameters = list(Phi = list(formula = phi), p = list(formula = p)))))
  m
}
m0 <- fit(~1, ~1)
m0$results$reals
```

Annual survival is about 0.56 and the recapture probability about 0.90,
Lebreton et al.'s numbers. A high $p$ is why the dipper is a good teaching
table: few animals are alive and missed, so the naive and model-based
answers are close, and the interesting structure is in $\phi$.

### Lebreton's flood

A flood in the spring of 1983 hit the study streams. Lebreton et al. compared
a model in which survival differs in the two intervals around it
(1982 to 1983 and 1983 to 1984) against constant and fully time-varying
survival, and against a sex effect.

```{r}
#| label: fit-set
ddl$Phi$flood <- as.integer(ddl$Phi$time %in% c(2, 3))
models <- list(
  "phi(.) p(.)"     = m0,
  "phi(flood) p(.)" = fit(~flood, ~1),
  "phi(sex) p(.)"   = fit(~sex, ~1),
  "phi(t) p(.)"     = fit(~time, ~1),
  "phi(t) p(t)"     = fit(~time, ~time))
aic <- data.frame(model = names(models),
                  k = sapply(models, function(m) length(unlist(m$results$beta))),
                  AIC = sapply(models, function(m) m$results$AIC))
aic$dAIC <- aic$AIC - min(aic$AIC)
knitr::kable(aic[order(aic$AIC), ], row.names = FALSE, digits = 1)
unique(predict(models[["phi(flood) p(.)"]])$Phi[, c("flood", "estimate", "lcl", "ucl")])
```

The flood model wins: survival of about 0.61 in ordinary years and 0.47 in
the flood years, with no support for a sex difference and nothing gained by
letting every year have its own survival. The fully time-varying model pays
for parameters that are, in part, not identified (the last $\phi$ and $p$
come only as a product).

### Does the model fit?

The standard goodness-of-fit battery for CJS (Pradel, Gimenez and Lebreton
2005; implemented in U-CARE and in `R2ucare`) breaks the deviation from the
fully time-dependent model into components with a biological reading. Test
3.SR asks whether newly marked animals are seen again as often as previously
marked ones; a failure means **transients**, animals passing through, or
animals marked young with lower first-year survival. Test 2.CT asks whether
being caught now changes the chance of being caught next time; a failure
means **trap dependence**. Tests 3.SM and 2.CL are the remaining, less
specific components; the four sum to an overall statistic whose ratio to its
degrees of freedom is the overdispersion factor $\hat c$.

```{r}
#| label: gof
X <- as.matrix(M[, -(1:2)])
g <- overall_CJS(X, rep(1, nrow(X)))
g
c(test3sr = test3sr(X, rep(1, nrow(X)))$test3sr[["p_val"]],
  test2ct = test2ct(X, rep(1, nrow(X)))$test2ct[["p_val"]])
```

The dipper passes, with $\hat c$ = `r fmt(g$chi2 / g$degree_of_freedom)`,
no sign of transients, and trap dependence just short of the 5% line: the
model's assumptions hold for this table about as well as they ever do.
Most of the corpus will not be this tidy.

## The same model across the corpus

eco holds 27 more capture-history tables that fit the model as they are or
after collapsing secondary occasions:
seabirds, geese and a tyrant flycatcher; sea lions, fin whales, elephant
seals and bottlenose dolphins; grass snakes, rattlesnakes and terrapins; a
frog; three species of stream fish; a damselfly and three populations of a
fritillary butterfly; and five species of plant. The companion script
[`cjs_corpus_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/cjs_corpus_compute.R)
fits the same three models to each and runs the U-CARE tests; it caches the
results in `cjs_data/cjs_corpus.rds` because the two Macquarie Island
elephant seal tables, with 7,500 and 18,000 animals, take a few minutes.

Turning a table into a history matrix needs three rules, all of which follow
from the standard:

- **Rows before first capture are dropped.** CJS conditions on first capture.
- **A missing row after first capture is not a miss.** The standard says a
  row exists exactly when the animal was at risk of being recorded (E4.4), so
  a gap is an animal that could not have been seen (a branded sea lion pup in
  a year with no resighting effort, a bird removed after capture). It enters
  the history as a 0 with $p$ fixed at 0 for that animal and occasion, so it
  says nothing about survival.
- **Robust-design tables are collapsed to the period.** Where a period has
  several secondary occasions (the brant, the Marion Island seals, the two
  dolphin studies, the frog), an animal counts as seen in the period if it
  was seen on any occasion.

The time between periods comes from each table's `__periods`: years for
annual studies, months for the stream fish and the frog, season dates for the
Bunbury dolphins, the authors' own MARK intervals for the rattlesnakes, and
search days for the two within-season insect studies. The Brazilian
flycatcher's session dates were not deposited, so its survival is per
session. Every $\phi$ below is per year unless the table says otherwise.

The models are $\phi(\cdot)\,p(\cdot)$; $\phi(\cdot)\,p(t)$, because effort is
never constant across years; and $\phi(\text{tsm})\,p(t)$, which gives the
first interval after marking its own survival (time since marking; Pradel et
al. 1997). The last is the standard response to a failed test 3.SR, and the
right comparison across species: in a table of animals marked as pups or
chicks, the first interval is juvenile survival and the rest is adult
survival.

```{r}
#| label: corpus-load
cache <- "cjs_data/cjs_corpus.rds"
have_corpus <- file.exists(cache)
if (have_corpus) {
  corpus <- readRDS(cache)
  f <- as.data.table(corpus$fits)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: corpus-table
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr have_corpus
f[, chat := gof_chi2 / gof_df]
f[, best := c("phi(.) p(.)", "phi(.) p(t)", "phi(tsm) p(t)")[apply(cbind(aic_a, aic_b, aic_c), 1, which.min)]]
tab <- f[order(taxon_group, -n_ind), .(table, group = taxon_group, animals = n_ind, periods = n_periods,
          per = interval_unit, `naive phi` = naive_phi, `phi(.)` = phi_a, `p(.)` = p_a,
          `phi later` = phi_later, `phi first` = phi_first, best, `c-hat` = chat)]
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
```

Placeholder: the figures and their reading go here once

## Where this goes

Everything above changes by one piece of the state or observation process,
and eco carries tables for each.

- **More states.** Let the latent state be a site, a breeding status or a
  disease class instead of just alive, and CJS becomes the multistate
  (Arnason-Schwarz) model. The kittiwake, penguin, Dolly Varden and Bunbury
  female-calf tables are multistate histories (`responseType` `state`), fit
  with `marked`'s `"Multistrata"` model or with `nimbleEcology`.
- **Closed sessions inside open years.** The robust-design tables collapsed
  above keep their secondary occasions in the table; Pollock's robust design
  uses them to estimate abundance within each period and temporary
  emigration between periods.
- **Space.** The spatial capture-recapture tables (`_scr`) add the trap at
  which each animal was caught, and estimate density instead of survival.

and [`cjs_corpus_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/cjs_corpus_compute.R)
in the eco repository. Data were read with `eco_set_version(10)`, so a later

```{r}
v <- eco_version()
cat(sprintf("eco version %s (Redivis eco %s, eco_meta %s, released %s)\n",
```

References. Cormack, R. M. (1964). Estimates of survival from the sighting of
marked animals. *Biometrika* 51, 429–438. Jolly, G. M. (1965). Explicit
estimates from capture-recapture data with both death and
immigration-stochastic model. *Biometrika* 52, 225–247. Seber, G. A. F.
(1965). A note on the multiple-recapture census. *Biometrika* 52, 249–259.
Lebreton, J.-D., Burnham, K. P., Clobert, J. and Anderson, D. R. (1992).
Modeling survival and testing biological hypotheses using marked animals: a

Capture-recapture survival models taking account of transients. *Biometrics*
53, 60–72. Pradel, R., Gimenez, O. and Lebreton, J.-D. (2005). Principles and
